title: Burnham Rules Out Northern Ireland Border Poll on First Visit, Sparking Sinn Féin Rebuke
detail: On his first official visit to Northern Ireland as Prime Minister on 27 August 2026, Andy Burnham told reporters in Belfast that a border poll on Irish unity was 'off the table,' saying: 'I will take a collaborative approach but some issues will be off the table, and that is one issue that will be off the table.' He pointed to the divisions left by the Brexit and Scottish independence referendums, arguing the government's focus should be on cost-of-living pressures and agreeing a Stormont budget rather than a fresh constitutional referendum. Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald rejected the remarks, saying Burnham had no authority to override the Good Friday Agreement's provision guaranteeing the people of Northern Ireland the right to determine their constitutional future, calling it a right that 'cannot be cast aside' by a UK prime minister. The Democratic Unionist Party welcomed Burnham's comments, with leader Gavin Robinson saying the PM had settled speculation over holding such a referendum. The visit, accompanied by Northern Ireland Secretary Chris Bryant, coincided with a stop at a wedding reception in Cultra, Co Down.

media.caption: PM Andy Burnham ruled out a Northern Ireland border poll during his first official visit to Belfast

title: Joint Committee on Human Rights: 40 Children Who Vanished From Asylum Hotels Still Not Found
detail: The Joint Committee on Human Rights reported on 27 August 2026 that 40 of the more than 470 unaccompanied asylum-seeking children who went missing from Home Office asylum hotels since 2023 remain unaccounted for, calling it a 'significant child protection failure.' Of the 472 children who disappeared, 432 have since been located, with the outstanding figure falling from 118 in 2024 to 78 in 2025 to 40 now; all but two of the remaining 40 are believed to have since turned 18. Former minister Angela Eagle said some recovered children had been 'located in exploitative situations and may have been trafficked or victims of other forms of exploitation.' England's Children's Commissioner Dame Rachel de Souza called the disappearances 'an unacceptable failure' and demanded the government set out what action it is taking. The cross-party committee wrote to the Home Secretary demanding quarterly updates on efforts to locate the remaining children and to explain why the disappearances occurred, noting the practice of housing lone child asylum seekers in hotels was ruled unlawful by the High Court in 2023.

sources.name: UK Parliament Joint Committee on Human Rights

media.caption: Forty children who went missing from UK asylum hotels since 2023 remain unaccounted for, a parliamentary committee found
